name: French Defence
goal: As Black against 1.e4, you can play the French Defence and know the plan against White's pawn chain: attack its base with ...c5 and your pieces, and keep ...f6 as a second break against its front.
intro: In the French Defence, 1...e6 and 2...d5, you let White build a big centre and then attack it. In the Advance Variation, White pushes a pawn to e5, making a chain of pawns on d4 and e5 that takes space on the kingside. Your plan is the same in every line where White pushes to e5: hit the base of the chain, its back pawn on d4, with ...c5 and your pieces. Hitting its front, e5, with ...f6 is a second way to break the chain, but it needs the right moment, because it opens lines for White too. The price is the bishop on c8, which stays shut in behind the e6 pawn for a while.

parts.title: The Advance Variation
parts.keyIdea: Against a pawn chain, attack its base first, with a pawn and then your pieces, and free your shut-in pieces while White's stay tied to it.
parts.text: You are Black, from White's first move. White pushes the e-pawn on to e5, the Advance Variation, and builds a chain of pawns whose front pawn stands in your half of the board. At each move, ask what your move does against White's chain of pawns and for your pieces.
parts.line: e4 e6 d4 d5 e5 c5 c3 Nc6 Nf3 Qb6 Be2 cxd4 cxd4 Nge7 Na3 Nf5 Nc2 Bd7 O-O Rc8

notes.text: 1...e6 gets ready for ...d5, with the e6 pawn ready to take back if White ever captures on d5. Your centre stays solid. The cost is that the bishop on c8 is shut in behind the e6 pawn for now.
2...d5 attacks the pawn on e4. White can defend it (3.Nc3 or 3.Nd2), trade with 3.exd5, which leaves a calm position with the same pawns for both sides, or push past with 3.e5, the Advance Variation.
3.e5 makes a chain: the d4 pawn holds up e5, and e5 takes space and the f6 square from your knight. 3...c5 hits the base of the chain, the d4 pawn. If that pawn goes, nothing holds up e5.
4.c3 backs up d4 with another pawn. 4...Nc6 brings a second attacker to d4, the knight joining the c5 pawn, and develops a piece.
5.Nf3 defends d4 again. 5...Qb6 lines up behind the c5 pawn, so once that pawn has taken on d4, the queen attacks d4 too. It also hits the pawn on b2, which only the bishop on c1 defends.
6.Be2 gets ready to castle. 6...cxd4 trades pawns on d4, and after 7.cxd4 White's c-pawn has gone, so from now on only pieces can defend d4. The c-file is also open for your rook later.
7...Nge7 brings the other knight out. It cannot use f6, which the e5 pawn covers, so it heads for f5, where it will be one more piece aimed at d4.

8.Na3 is on its way to c2 to help d4. 8...Nf5: now three of your pieces attack d4 (both knights and the queen) and only two defend it (the knight on f3 and the queen), so White has to find another defender at once. If White castles at once instead, with 8.O-O, the same move leaves d4 attacked three times and defended twice, and the Engine clearly prefers your side.

9.Nc2 holds d4 for now, with three defenders against your three attackers, so nothing is won by force yet. 9...Bd7 brings out the bishop that the e6 pawn shut in, and it is one of the Engine's top choices. Hitting the front of the chain at once with 9...f6 was possible, but the Engine rates it about 0.4 of a pawn lower. One reason is that when the lines open, your king is still in the centre and your bishop is still shut in. Finish developing first, then look again at ...f6.

10.O-O puts White's king in safety. 10...Rc8 puts your rook on the c-file, which is open because both c-pawns are gone, lined up behind your knight on c6 against the white knight on c2. Your knights and queen are aimed at d4, your bishop is out and your rook is on the open file, while White's pieces are tied to d4. Your king and kingside still need to catch up. The chain still stands, so keep the pressure on its base and pick the moment for ...f6 with care.
